newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine opposition join forces against Ramos.
newsitem.headline: Philippine opposition join forces against Ramos.

text.p: Three Philippine opposition parties on Wednesday fired the first shot of the 1998 presidential battle by joining forces after the Supreme Court effectively barred President Fidel Ramos from running for a second term.
The unity pact brought together the country's most popular politician, Vice-President Joseph Estrada, its largest opposition party and another group headed by the Senate president.

"We will win...we will win," Laban (Fight) party chief Edgardo Angara said after signing the merger agreement with Estrada's Party of the Filipino Masses (PMP) and the Nationalist People's Coalition Party.

The three groups set up the alliance, called Fight of the Nationalist Filipino Masses (LMMP), a day after the Supreme Court barred a petition to change the 10-year-old constitution to allow Ramos to run in the May 1998 polls.
Though it has the resources to set up a powerful nationwide political machine, the alliance's failure to rope in two other opposition heavyweights could weaken its chances, analysts said.
The two that did not join, at least for the moment, were Senator Gloria Macapagal Arroyo, another leading presidential contender, and Senator Miriam Santiago.

Arroyo, an economist and daughter of a late president, is closely behind Estrada in opinion polls. Santiago narrowly lost to Ramos in a seven-way presidential contest in 1992 and remains popular among the youth.
"That's only temporary," Angara told a news conference. "We believe that all opposition of note will ultimately join this group. It's only a matter of time."
The presidential palace dismissed the new alliance.
"We don't think they would provide a formidable opponent, not even Estrada," said Ramos's executive secretary, Ruben Torres.
The constitution, written in 1987 after the 20-year hardline rule of Ferdinand Marcos collapsed, limits presidents to one six-year term.
Although Ramos has denied he is interested in a second term, his aides have been linked to the campaign to amend the charter so he could run again.

Knocked out of the race by the Supreme Court, Ramos is expected to focus his efforts on picking a candidate to ensure the victory of the administration Lakas ng Bayan (People's Party) in the 1998 polls. He is expected to announce his choice later in the year.
Three men seeking Ramos's so-called "anointment" are Finance Secretary Roberto de Ocampo, defence chief Renato de Villa and Lower House Speaker Jose de Venecia.
"Their days are numbered," Estrada said in a speech after the signing of the unity accord.
The Supreme Court verdict cheered the stock market, helping push the main index up 12.63 points to 2,787.74 by the close.
"It means there's political stability," said Elline Salvatierra, analyst at Dharmala Securities.
Economic analysts said they will miss Ramos, who has been credited with turning the country from "sick man of Asia" to a vibrant economy, but say the decision was probably for the best.
